transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-28
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Emily Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Marquez (Redwood SE), Lisa Grant (Novapay Head of ML), Aaron Cho (Novapay SRE), Maya Patel (Novapay Product)

Summary: quick sync on POC latency numbers; focused on TTFT (time-to-first-token), streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs, observed tail sequence length, and kernel selection (quantized kernels, cutlass/triton path). Action items to run targeted benchmarks and share sequence distribution.

Topics: latency numbers, TTFT optimizations, streaming behavior, sequence length distribution, kernel choices, caching (KV cache), batching, dedicated vs hosted capacity decisions.

Transcript:
00:00 Emily Chen: okay hey everyone thanks for joining we are on for the weekly POC sync for NovaPay, quick note Diego and I will run through the latest TTFT numbers and some kernel ideas, Lisa feel free to jump in with new data
00:32 Lisa Grant: thanks yeah um we've been seeing increased latency spikes on long receipts flows last week, 95th percentile token length went up to around 840 tokens on some paths so that probably explains tail
01:05 Diego Marquez: got it, and when you say 840 is that input tokens or total tokens with context plus response?
01:18 Lisa Grant: sorry that's total tokens combined, average prompt is more like 110 but some workflows append transaction history so that pushes it up
01:45 Emily Chen: okay that matches what we saw; quick note on TTFT -- on hosted we measured median TTFT ~120ms, P50 around 115, but the big stuff is the P95 which hit 420ms in non-streamed mode
02:12 Aaron Cho: are those numbers with KV cache warm or cold? we saw cold starts earlier in morning maintenance
02:28 Diego Marquez: good question, these were mixed; the benchmark had a warm KV cache for prefixes we commonly hit, but cold path (first request for a user) goes up to about 850ms TTFT because kernel compilation and CL scheduling differences happen
03:00 Maya Patel: hmm so streaming helps here? we saw partial tokens come in faster in the demo last week
03:20 Diego Marquez: yes streaming reduces perceived TTFT because the server can flush first tokens as soon as decoding starts; in our tests enabling streaming dropped time-to-first-byte by ~70-80ms on average and reduced P95 by ~50-80ms depending on batch config
03:55 Lisa Grant: that's promising; what's the tradeoff on cost or throughput?
04:12 Diego Marquez: tradeoff is small CPU overhead for chunked sends, and slightly lower batching efficiency if you make very tiny stream chunks. For high throughput we recommend continuous batching + streaming with a short debounce (we use 20-50ms) so batching remains effective
05:00 Emily Chen: also kernel choice matters: on A10/p4 type hardware the cutlass path with int8 quantization gave good latency for short sequences, but for long sequences the triton kernel with fused attention did better by avoiding O(n^2) memory copies
05:36 Lisa Grant: we use quantized models in the POC, we saw some accuracy drift but it's within acceptable range, said the product team
06:00 Emily Chen: right and for TTFT the quantized kernels need to be preloaded; we saw extra 60-120ms on cold starts because we swap kernels on first invocation if not resident
06:25 Aaron Cho: can we pin kernels or preload during ramp? we have a warm pool concept in our infra
06:40 Diego Marquez: yes that's a great pattern -- preload kernels at deploy time and keep a warm instance; Redwood Dedicated supports keeping reserved pools with pinned kernels which avoids that cold penalty, and there's also a startup lifecycle hook we can use in Private deployments to instantiate the kernels at boot
07:12 Lisa Grant: about sequence length distribution -- we'll share the CSV, but practically 75% of requests are under 150 tokens, 90% under 320, 95th around 840 as I said earlier, and the outliers are the receipts with full itemized history
07:45 Emily Chen: perfect that helps; for tuning we recommend two profiles: short-seq profile (<=256) with cutlass int8 + aggressive batching and streaming enabled, and long-seq profile (>256) with triton/fused attention, higher memory allocation and KV cache optimizations
08:20 Maya Patel: can the model/router pick profile automatically?
08:36 Diego Marquez: yes we can route by estimated sequence length at request time; Redwood's smart routing can pick a model variant or kernel profile by a heuristic on sequence length in header, and fallback if capacity is constrained
09:02 Lisa Grant: what about TTFT when model does function/tool calling — we have a chain of calls and sometimes that adds latency
09:18 Emily Chen: function calls add round trips, streaming helps because you can stream intermediate tokens while the tool executes but depending on how you implement tooling it can add 50-200ms; we typically recommend batching tool invocations when possible and using local microservices to reduce network hops
09:50 Aaron Cho: on your suggested benchmark, what environment should we run? cloud hosted or our dedicated staging infra?
10:03 Diego Marquez: for apples-to-apples, run both: 1) hosted Redwood API with streaming enabled and with the same prompt set, 2) Dedicated-like instance (we can spin a reserved pool for the pilot) with preloaded kernels. We'll provide the benchmark harness (curl scripts and node client)
10:36 Lisa Grant: ok we'll run hosted first then Dedicated staging next week
11:00 Emily Chen: noted. Some notes on batching: we found continuous batching with adaptive debounce gives best p50 while preserving throughput, but if you need lowest P95 you can tradeoff throughput for smaller batch windows or use model sharding to reduce per-request queuing
11:40 Diego Marquez: also KV cache helps for repeated prefixes; in your logs I saw heat around a few merchant templates so we can prime KV cache for those top templates to reduce re-computation and TTFT by caching past KVs
12:05 Lisa Grant: do we see any regression when caching is on? we were worried about stale context
12:20 Emily Chen: cache invalidation policy is config-driven; we recommend time-based TTL plus event-driven invalidation when transaction history updates -- that keeps cache warm and consistent
12:40 Maya Patel: quick question on tooling: can we get token-level timing breakdowns? our PMs want per-token latency to debug spikes
12:55 Diego Marquez: yes Redwood Console exposes per-token timing plus route/model breakdowns; we'll share a dashboard link and CSV export so you can map spikes to prompts
13:20 Lisa Grant: great, also we have SOC2 questions next week -- security review call with our compliance team
13:35 Emily Chen: we can schedule that; I'll include our security pack and SOC2 report in the follow-up
13:50 Aaron Cho: back to kernels: you mentioned warm-up cost for quantized kernels is significant, what about pre-quantized images to avoid on-the-fly quantization?
14:08 Diego Marquez: pre-quantized model artifacts are best practice; we can provision model artifact variants (int8, int4) during onboarding and load them directly to avoid quantization latency. That reduces cold kernel swaps
14:40 Lisa Grant: good to know. For the POC pilot duration, is 4 weeks enough to see steady-state?
14:58 Emily Chen: usually 3-4 weeks is adequate; first week for baseline and kernel warm-up, second for tuning, third for stress and SLO validation, fourth for run-rate numbers and contract discussions
15:20 Maya Patel: any gotchas on streaming and mobile clients? we have some Android/ios clients that rely on chunked payloads
15:36 Diego Marquez: mobile streaming is fine but watch for jitter and reassembly; use a small chunk size and client-side buffering for smooth UX; also consider gRPC streaming for better reliability vs raw HTTP chunked
15:58 Lisa Grant: okay what do you need from us to run the bench?
16:12 Emily Chen: the prompt set (top 100), sequence-length CSV, and a credential for a test API key (we can use obfuscated keys) — Diego will share the harness and scripts
16:30 Lisa Grant: we'll share the data by Friday 2026-05-01
16:45 Diego Marquez: noted, I'll set up the hosted run and the dedicated warm pool for the week of 2026-05-04
17:00 Emily Chen: quick recap and next steps: Diego to run TTFT + streaming benchmarks (due 2026-05-05), Lisa to share sequences and prompts (due 2026-05-01), Emily to send pricing and SOC2/security pack and kernel config notes (due 2026-05-03). We'll schedule security review with compliance next week. Any final Qs?
17:28 Lisa Grant: none here thanks everyone
17:35 Maya Patel: thanks
17:40 Emily Chen: thanks all, end call

Notes and artifacts referenced:
